title: The Supreme Court of Israel
hook: A court that built constitutional review out of ordinary statutes, opened its doors to almost any petitioner — and is now, for the first time, itself the central issue in a national election.
key_points: Israel has no single written constitution; the Knesset instead enacts 'Basic Laws' meant to serve as constitutional chapters.
The 1995 Mizrahi Bank ruling treated those Basic Laws as a constitution, claiming the power to strike down conflicting legislation — its Marbury moment.
The court wears two hats: highest court of appeal, and High Court of Justice hearing petitions directly against the government.
Its docket is non-discretionary and huge — over 11,000 new filings in 2024, including 2,892 High Court of Justice petitions.
Access is wide but success is rare: it largely abolished strict standing rules, yet reverses the government in fewer than 10% of cases.
A nine-member committee picks justices, and since 2008 appointments need seven votes — a professional veto the 2023 overhaul sought to remove.
content_html: Israel offers a useful test of a question most civics courses skip: can a country have constitutional judicial review without a constitution? It has never enacted one. Instead the Knesset passes "Basic Laws," intended as chapters of a constitution to be completed later. In the 1995 Mizrahi Bank decision the Supreme Court held those Basic Laws already function as the constitutional framework — and therefore that it could strike down ordinary legislation conflicting with the rights they protect. Writing for SCOTUSblog, Zachary Shemtob calls it Israel's Marbury v. Madison moment.
extra_html:
What followed looks paradoxical. The court opened access dramatically, all but abandoning strict standing and justiciability rules from the early 1980s onward, and it takes petitions against the government directly in its capacity as the High Court of Justice — over 11,000 new filings in 2024, none of which it can decline. Yet it uses the power sparingly: only 25 statutory provisions struck since 1995, government action reversed in under 10% of cases, and dissents in roughly 1% of three-justice panels.

That combination — wide access, restrained outcomes, and a selection committee where a seven-of-nine supermajority gives sitting judges and the bar an effective veto — is what the 2023 overhaul proposal targeted. It would have given the coalition control of appointments, added a legislative override, and abolished "reasonableness" review; the resulting protests were the largest in Israel's history. The court struck down the reasonableness amendment 8-7 in January 2024, holding it could review amendments to Basic Laws themselves. Shemtob describes the aftermath as unresolved: four seats unfilled, a chief justice the government refuses to recognize, and the court's own fate on the ballot.

related.title: The Supreme Court of Japan
related.hook: Japan's top court has the power of constitutional review and almost never uses it: roughly ten laws struck down in eighty years, against 900-plus in the United States.

related.title: The Constitutional Court of South Africa
related.hook: Born out of the end of apartheid, this court was designed to make a new constitution stick — and became one of the world's most-cited voices on what rights a government owes its people.

related.title: The European Court of Justice
related.hook: A court above nations: it doesn't replace any country's supreme court, but it makes sure EU law means the same thing in every member state.

related.title: The Judiciary & Judicial Review
related.hook: Courts don't just settle disputes between people — through judicial review, many can also strike down a law or an official act that violates the constitution.

related.title: Democratic Backsliding
related.hook: Democracies rarely die in a single coup anymore. More often they erode — legally, gradually, step by step — until little is left but the shell of elections.

flashcards.prompt: Without a written constitution, where does Israel's Supreme Court find authority to strike down legislation?
flashcards.back_html: From the Basic Laws. In Mizrahi Bank (1995) the court held they form Israel's constitutional framework, so ordinary statutes violating the rights they protect can be invalidated.

flashcards.prompt: What does it mean that the court sits as the 'High Court of Justice'?

choices.text: It hears petitions against government bodies directly, as a court of first instance
It reviews only criminal appeals from the district courts
It is a separate constitutional court with different judges

flashcards.explanation_html: Alongside its appellate role, the same court takes original petitions against ministers, the military and state authorities — which is why its caseload is so large and non-discretionary.

flashcards.prompt: Why is the composition of the judicial selection committee the core of the overhaul fight?
flashcards.back_html: Since 2008 an appointment needs seven of nine votes, so judges and bar representatives can block a purely political pick. Changing the membership would hand the governing coalition control of who joins the court.
